idiom_name: value semantics with copy-on-write storage sharing; static let or factory pool for identity-bearing flyweights
implementation_notes: Swift's value types already share their storage: String, Array and Dictionary keep their buffer in a reference-counted box and copy only on mutation (copy-on-write), so passing values around does not duplicate the data; the classic flyweight is largely absorbed by the memory model, and the extrinsic state is just another stored property. What remains to write by hand is the pool for identity-bearing shared state: a static let for lazily initialised process-wide instances, a factory holding a Dictionary keyed by the intrinsic state, and a final class (or a struct wrapping one) when two contexts must observe the same instance. Immutability comes from let and from exposing no mutating API.
pitfalls: Copy-on-write only pays while the value is not mutated: one write into a shared struct copies the whole buffer, so the sharing silently degenerates into duplication unless the flyweight is treated as immutable.
A static var pool is not thread-safe by itself; concurrent use needs a lock, a serial queue or actor isolation, and a static stored property inside a generic type exists once per specialization.

A struct holding a class shares that reference on copy, so value semantics do not protect a class-backed flyweight from mutation: make the class immutable (let fields only) or keep everything in value types.
Pool keys must have structural equality (Hashable synthesized from the intrinsic fields); an identity-based key type creates duplicate flyweights for equal states.
